items.simple_meaning: Information is facts or details about something.
items.explanation: When you learn facts about a topic, you are getting information. We can find information in books, from teachers, or by asking questions.
items.example_sentence: Our teacher gave us information about the school trip to the planetarium.
items.real_world_usage: I need more information about tigers for my project.
items.spelling_guidance: Break it into parts: in-for-ma-tion. It ends with '-tion', which sounds like 'shun'.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'information' to talk about finding and sharing facts.
items.illustration_brief: A child in a school library reading a large book about animals, with small floating picture bubbles of a tiger, an elephant and a map around the book.

items.simple_meaning: History is the study of things that happened in the past.
items.explanation: History tells us about people, places and events from long ago. In history lessons, we learn how people lived in earlier times.
items.example_sentence: In our history class, we learnt how people built forts long ago.
items.real_world_usage: History is my favourite subject because I love stories about the past.
items.spelling_guidance: Remember the 'y' at the end: his-to-ry. Don't forget the 'o' in the middle.
items.learning_objective: Children will understand 'history' as learning about the past and use it in school contexts.
items.illustration_brief: A classroom with a timeline poster on the wall showing an old fort, a bullock cart and a steam train, while children look at it with interest.

items.simple_meaning: A minute is a unit of time equal to sixty seconds.
items.explanation: There are sixty minutes in one hour. We use minutes to measure short amounts of time, like how long it takes to brush our teeth.
items.example_sentence: The school bus will arrive in five minutes, so please pack your tiffin quickly.
items.real_world_usage: Can I play for ten more minutes, please?
items.spelling_guidance: It is spelt min-ute, with 'ute' at the end even though it sounds like 'it'.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'minute' to measure and talk about short periods of time.
items.illustration_brief: A large round wall clock with the minute hand highlighted, beside a child waiting at a school bus stop with a backpack.

items.simple_meaning: A computer is a machine that stores information and helps us do tasks like typing, drawing and calculating.
items.explanation: A computer follows instructions to help us work, learn and play. It has a screen, a keyboard and a mouse.
items.example_sentence: We typed a short story on the computer in our school lab.
items.real_world_usage: I learnt how to draw shapes on the computer today.
items.spelling_guidance: Split it into com-pu-ter. It ends in '-er'.
items.learning_objective: Children will name a computer and describe how it is used for learning.
items.illustration_brief: Children sitting at desks in a bright school computer lab, one child using a mouse while a colourful drawing appears on the screen.

items.simple_meaning: A manager is a person who is in charge of a shop, team or workplace.
items.explanation: A manager plans the work and helps the people in a team do their jobs well. A bank, a hotel or a cricket team can have a manager.
items.example_sentence: The bank manager helped Papa open a savings account for me.
items.real_world_usage: The manager of the shop helped us find the right size.
items.spelling_guidance: Think of the word 'manage' and add 'r': manage + r = manager.
items.learning_objective: Children will understand that a manager leads and organises work in a place.
items.illustration_brief: A friendly manager at a bank counter showing a form to a parent and child, with staff working at desks in the background.

items.simple_meaning: A scene is one part of a play, film or story that happens in one place.
items.explanation: A play is made of many scenes. Each scene shows what happens at one place and time in the story.
items.example_sentence: In the school play, I acted in the scene where the clever rabbit tricks the lion.
items.real_world_usage: The forest scene was my favourite part of the drama.
items.spelling_guidance: Scene has a silent 'c': s-c-e-n-e. It sounds like 'seen'.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'scene' to describe a part of a play or story.
items.illustration_brief: Children performing on a school stage with a painted forest backdrop, one dressed as a rabbit and another as a lion, with an audience watching.

items.simple_meaning: To spend means to use money to buy things.
items.explanation: When you spend money, you give it to someone to get something you want or need. It is wise to spend money carefully.
items.example_sentence: I will spend my pocket money on new colour pencils for Diwali drawings.
items.real_world_usage: I don't want to spend all my money at the fair.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'spend' to talk about using money and making choices.
items.illustration_brief: A child at a small stationery shop counter handing coins to the shopkeeper in exchange for a box of colour pencils.

items.simple_meaning: Material is cloth used to make clothes and other things.
items.explanation: Clothes are made from different materials like cotton, silk or wool. Some materials are soft and light, while others are thick and warm.
items.example_sentence: Mummy bought soft cotton material to stitch my new kurta for the festival.
items.spelling_guidance: Break it into ma-te-ri-al. It ends with '-al'.
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'material' to talk about the cloth that clothes are made from.
items.illustration_brief: A cloth shop with colourful rolls of cotton and silk material stacked on shelves, and a child touching a soft piece of fabric.

items.simple_meaning: A direction is the way something is moving or facing.
items.explanation: Directions tell us which way to go, like north, south, left or right. A compass helps us find the right direction.
items.example_sentence: On our trip to the hill station, Papa checked the map to find the right direction.
items.real_world_usage: Which direction is the railway station?
items.learning_objective: Children will use 'direction' to talk about which way to go when travelling.
items.illustration_brief: A family car paused by a road signpost with arrows pointing different ways, and a child holding a map and a compass.

items.simple_meaning: A museum is a building where interesting old or special objects are kept for people to see.
items.explanation: In a museum, you can see things like old coins, paintings, tools and even dinosaur bones. People visit museums to learn about history, art and science.
items.example_sentence: Our class went to the museum to see old coins and ancient pots.
items.real_world_usage: I saw a huge dinosaur skeleton at the museum!
items.spelling_guidance: Spell it mu-se-um. It ends with '-um', not '-ium'.
items.learning_objective: Children will describe a museum as a place to see and learn about special objects.
items.illustration_brief: A group of school children with a guide looking at a glass case of ancient pots and coins inside a bright museum hall, with a dinosaur skeleton in the background.
